title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
summary: How Saudi Arabia removes salt from seawater using heat or a membrane, and the energy and brine challenges this creates.
poll: Turning seawater into drinking water is worth the energy it costs.

versions.title: Water From the Sea
versions.text:
The sea is big. But we can not drink it. Seawater has lots of salt. Salt makes you thirst more.

Fresh water has just a bit of salt. It is what we drink. There is not much of it.

Saudi Arabia is hot and dry. It has no lakes or streams. It does not get much rain. So it takes the salt out of seawater.

One way is to heat the sea. Steam goes up. The salt stays down. The steam cools. Now it is fresh. Rain is made like this too.

The next way is to use a filter. A strong pump pushes the sea in. The filter has tiny holes. Drops get through. Salt does not. Most new plants use this way.

Some salt is left. It goes back to the sea. It must be spread out. That keeps fish safe.

This work needs lots of power. The sun can help.

Long pipes take the fresh drink to towns. Some goes far, to Riyadh.

It is hard work to make fresh water. So do not waste it!

versions.title: Water From the Sea
versions.text:
Look at the sea. It holds lots and lots of water. But you can not drink it. Seawater has too much salt in it. Salt water would make you more thirsty.

Most of the water on Earth is in the sea. Fresh water has very little salt. That is the water we drink. There is not much of it on Earth.

Saudi Arabia is a hot, dry land. It has no rivers. It gets very little rain. So the country takes the salt out of seawater.

One way to do this is with heat. The water gets hot, and steam rises. The salt stays behind. Then the steam cools down. It turns into fresh water. This is a lot like how rain forms.

The second way uses a filter. A strong pump pushes seawater at it. The filter has tiny holes. Water can pass through, but the salt can not. Most new plants use this way.

Some very salty water is left. It goes back to the sea. It must be spread out so fish stay safe.

These big plants need lots of power. People now try to use power from the sun.

Long pipes take the water to towns and cities. Some of it goes far, all the way to Riyadh.

Making fresh water is hard work. That is why we should not waste it.

versions.title: Turning Seawater Into Drinking Water
versions.text:
Imagine you stand on a beach on the Red Sea. The water stretches all the way to the sky, yet you can't drink one cup of it. Seawater is so salty that it would make you even more thirsty.

Most of the water on Earth is in the sea. Only a small part is fresh water, which has very little salt. People need fresh water to drink, cook, and stay well.

Saudi Arabia is a hot, dry land with no rivers, and it gets very little rain. To solve this problem, the country takes the salt out of seawater. It has large water plants on its coasts.

One way to take out the salt uses heat. Seawater is heated until steam rises, and the salt is left behind. When the steam cools, it turns back into fresh water. This works much like the way rain forms.

The second way uses a special filter. Strong pumps push seawater against it. The holes in the filter are so tiny that water can squeeze through, but salt can't. Most new plants now use this way because it needs less power.

Some very salty water is left over. The plants send it back to the sea, but workers must spread it out so it does not harm fish.

These plants need a great deal of power. Saudi Arabia is now testing plants that use power from the sun.

Long pipes carry the fresh water to towns and cities. Some of it goes hundreds of kilometers to Riyadh.

Making fresh water from the sea takes hard work and a lot of power. That is why each drop is worth saving.

versions.title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
versions.text:
Picture yourself on a beach on the Red Sea coast. Water stretches all the way to the sky, yet you could not drink a single cup of it. Seawater is so salty that drinking it would make your body lose water. It would leave you even more thirsty.

About 97 percent of the water on Earth is in the oceans. Only a small part is fresh water, which has very little salt. Much of that fresh water is frozen in ice, so people can reach only a tiny amount of it.

Saudi Arabia has no rivers and gets very little rain. So the country depends on desalination, which means taking salt out of seawater. It is one of the biggest makers of this kind of water in the world. It has large plants on the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf.

One method uses heat. Seawater is boiled, and the steam rises while the salt stays behind. When the steam cools, it turns back into fresh water. This works much like rain, which forms when water rises from the sea and falls as fresh drops.

The second method uses a membrane, a thin sheet full of very tiny holes. Strong pumps push seawater against it with great pressure. Water squeezes through the holes, but the salt cannot. This method uses less energy, so most new plants choose it.

Both methods leave behind brine, which is very salty water. Plants send it back to the sea, but they must spread it out with care so it does not harm fish and coral.

Desalination needs a great deal of energy. Saudi Arabia is testing plants that run on power from the sun.

Long pipelines carry the water inland. Some of it travels hundreds of kilometers to reach Riyadh.

Since making fresh water takes so much work and energy, every drop is worth saving.

versions.title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
versions.text:
Standing on the Red Sea coast, you can gaze at water that stretches all the way to the horizon, yet you could not safely drink a single cup of it. Seawater contains so much dissolved salt that drinking it would actually draw water out of your body's cells, which would leave you far thirstier than before.

About 97 percent of the water on Earth is found in the oceans. Only a small portion is fresh water, and a large share of that is locked in glaciers and polar ice sheets, so people can reach only a tiny fraction of the planet's total supply.

Saudi Arabia has no rivers that flow all year and receives very little rainfall, which means that its natural sources of fresh water are extremely limited. For this reason, the kingdom depends heavily on desalination, the process of removing salt from seawater. It has become one of the largest producers of desalinated water in the world, with huge plants along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf.

The older of the two main methods is distillation, which relies on heat. Seawater is boiled, and the steam rises while the salt stays behind. When the steam cools, it condenses into fresh water. This process imitates the way rain forms, because water that evaporates from the ocean also leaves its salt behind.

The second method is reverse osmosis. Powerful pumps force seawater against a membrane, a thin sheet covered with extremely tiny openings, using tremendous pressure. Water molecules squeeze through the openings, while the dissolved salt cannot pass. Because reverse osmosis uses much less energy than distillation, most modern plants now prefer it.

Both methods produce brine, which is highly concentrated leftover salt water. Plants return it to the sea, but engineers must spread it out carefully, because a thick layer of brine can damage the marine ecosystem, including fish and coral reefs.

Desalination also requires an enormous amount of energy, much of which has traditionally come from burning fuel. To make the process more sustainable, Saudi Arabia is testing plants that are powered by sunlight.

Finally, long pipelines carry the purified water inland, and some of it travels hundreds of kilometers before it reaches Riyadh.

Because producing fresh water demands so much effort and energy, every drop deserves to be conserved.

versions.title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
versions.text:
Standing on the Red Sea coast, you can gaze at water that stretches uninterrupted to the horizon, yet you could not safely drink a single cup of it. Seawater contains such a high concentration of dissolved salt that drinking it would actually draw water out of your body's cells, which would leave you considerably thirstier than before.

Approximately 97 percent of the water on Earth is located in the oceans. Only a small portion is fresh water, and a substantial share of that is locked in glaciers and polar ice sheets, so people can access only a tiny fraction of the planet's total supply.

Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers and receives very little rainfall, which means that its natural sources of fresh water are extremely limited. Consequently, the kingdom relies heavily on desalination, the process of removing salt from seawater, and it has become one of the largest producers of desalinated water in the world, operating enormous facilities along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf.

The older of the two principal methods is distillation, which depends on heat. Seawater is boiled, and the steam rises while the salt remains behind. When the steam cools, it condenses into fresh water. This process imitates the natural formation of rain, because water that evaporates from the ocean also abandons its salt.

The second method is reverse osmosis. Powerful pumps force seawater against a membrane, a thin synthetic sheet perforated with microscopic openings, using tremendous pressure. Water molecules squeeze through the openings, while the dissolved salt particles cannot pass. Because reverse osmosis consumes considerably less energy than distillation, most contemporary plants now prefer it.

Both methods generate brine, which is highly concentrated leftover salt water. Plants return it to the sea, but engineers must disperse it carefully, because a dense layer of brine can damage the marine ecosystem, including fish and fragile coral reefs.

Desalination additionally requires an enormous quantity of energy, much of which has traditionally come from burning fossil fuels. To make the process more sustainable, Saudi Arabia is experimenting with facilities that are powered by solar energy.

Finally, extensive pipelines transport the purified water inland, and some of it travels hundreds of kilometers before it reaches Riyadh.

Because producing fresh water demands so much effort and energy, every drop deserves to be conserved.

versions.title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
versions.text:
Standing on the Red Sea coast, you can gaze at water that stretches uninterrupted to the horizon, yet you could not safely drink a single cup of it. Seawater contains such a high concentration of dissolved salt that consuming it would actually draw moisture out of your body's cells, which would ultimately leave you considerably thirstier than before.

Approximately 97 percent of the water on Earth is located in the oceans. Only a small portion is fresh water, and a substantial share of that is permanently locked in glaciers and polar ice sheets, so humanity can access only a tiny fraction of the planet's total supply.

Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers and receives remarkably little rainfall, which means that its natural sources of fresh water are extremely limited. Consequently, the kingdom relies heavily on desalination, the industrial process of removing salt from seawater, and it has become one of the largest producers of desalinated water in the world, operating enormous facilities along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf.

The older of the two principal methods is distillation, which depends on thermal energy. Seawater is boiled, and the resulting steam rises while the salt remains behind. When the steam cools, it condenses into fresh water. This procedure imitates the natural formation of rain, because water that evaporates from the ocean similarly abandons its salt.

The second method is reverse osmosis. Powerful pumps force seawater against a membrane, a thin synthetic sheet perforated with microscopic openings, applying tremendous pressure. Individual water molecules squeeze through the openings, whereas the dissolved salt particles are physically unable to pass. Because reverse osmosis consumes considerably less energy than distillation, most contemporary plants now favor it.

Both methods generate brine, which is highly concentrated leftover salt water. Facilities return it to the sea, but engineers must disperse it carefully, because a dense, undiluted layer of brine can damage the surrounding marine ecosystem, including fish and fragile coral reefs.

Desalination additionally requires an enormous quantity of energy, much of which has traditionally come from burning fossil fuels. To make the process more environmentally sustainable, Saudi Arabia is experimenting with facilities that are powered by solar energy.

Finally, extensive pipelines transport the purified water inland, and some of it travels hundreds of kilometers before it reaches the capital, Riyadh.

Because producing fresh water demands so much effort, investment, and energy, every individual drop deserves to be conserved.

versions.title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
versions.text:
Standing on the Red Sea coast, you can gaze at water that stretches uninterrupted to the horizon, yet you could not safely drink a single cup of it. Seawater contains such a high concentration of dissolved salt that consuming it would actually draw moisture out of your body's cells, which would ultimately leave you considerably thirstier than before.

Approximately 97 percent of the water on Earth is located in the oceans. Of the small remaining portion that qualifies as fresh water, a substantial share is permanently immobilized in glaciers and polar ice sheets, so humanity can actually reach only a tiny fraction of the planet's total supply.

Saudi Arabia possesses no permanent rivers and receives remarkably little precipitation, which means that its natural reserves of fresh water are extraordinarily limited. Consequently, the kingdom relies heavily on desalination, the industrial process of extracting salt from seawater. It has become one of the largest producers of desalinated water in the world, operating enormous facilities along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf.

The older of the two principal technologies is distillation, which depends on thermal energy. Seawater is boiled, and the resulting vapor rises while the salt remains behind, after which the vapor cools and condenses into fresh water. This procedure deliberately imitates the natural formation of rain, because water that evaporates from the ocean similarly abandons its dissolved minerals.

The second technology is reverse osmosis, in which powerful pumps force seawater against a membrane, a thin synthetic sheet perforated with microscopic openings, while applying tremendous pressure. Water molecules squeeze through the openings, whereas the dissolved salt particles are unable to pass. Because reverse osmosis consumes considerably less energy than distillation, most modern installations now favor it.

Both technologies generate brine, which is highly concentrated residual salt water. Facilities return it to the sea, but engineers must disperse it meticulously, because a dense, undiluted accumulation of brine can devastate the surrounding marine ecosystem, including fish populations and fragile coral reefs.

Desalination additionally requires an enormous quantity of energy, much of which has traditionally come from burning fossil fuels. To make the process more environmentally sustainable, Saudi Arabia is experimenting with facilities that are powered mainly by solar energy.

Finally, extensive pipelines transport the purified water inland, and some of it travels hundreds of kilometers before it eventually reaches the capital, Riyadh.

Because manufacturing fresh water demands such considerable effort, investment, and energy, every individual drop deserves to be carefully conserved.

versions.title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
versions.text:
Standing on the Red Sea coast, one can gaze upon water that stretches uninterrupted to the horizon, yet one could not safely drink even a single cup of it. Seawater contains such a formidable concentration of dissolved salt that consuming it would actually draw moisture out of the body's cells through osmosis, leaving the drinker considerably thirstier than before rather than relieving that thirst.

Approximately 97 percent of the water on Earth is located within the oceans. Of the comparatively small remaining portion that qualifies as fresh water, a substantial share is permanently immobilized within glaciers and polar ice sheets, meaning that humanity can realistically access only a minuscule fraction of the planet's total water supply.

Saudi Arabia possesses no permanent rivers and receives remarkably little precipitation, which means that its natural reserves of fresh water are extraordinarily limited. Consequently, the kingdom relies heavily upon desalination, the industrial process of extracting dissolved salt from seawater, and it has become one of the largest producers of desalinated water anywhere in the world, operating enormous facilities along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf coastlines.

The older of the two principal technologies is distillation, a method that depends fundamentally on thermal energy. Seawater is heated until it boils, and the resulting vapor rises while the dissolved salt remains behind in the original liquid; once this vapor subsequently cools, it condenses back into fresh water. This procedure deliberately imitates the natural formation of rain, since water that evaporates naturally from the ocean likewise abandons its dissolved minerals in the process.

The second technology is reverse osmosis, in which powerful pumps force seawater against a membrane, a thin synthetic sheet perforated with countless microscopic openings, while simultaneously applying tremendous pressure. Individual water molecules squeeze through these openings, whereas the dissolved salt particles are structurally unable to pass through at all. Because reverse osmosis consumes considerably less energy than distillation, the overwhelming majority of modern installations now favor this particular approach.

Both technologies inevitably generate brine, a highly concentrated residual salt water. Facilities return this brine to the sea, but engineers must disperse it meticulously, because a dense, undiluted accumulation can devastate the surrounding marine ecosystem, including fish populations and fragile coral reef communities that cannot tolerate such extreme salinity.

Desalination additionally requires an enormous quantity of energy, much of which has traditionally originated from burning fossil fuels. To render the process more environmentally sustainable, Saudi Arabia is experimenting with facilities powered substantially by solar energy, reducing the dependence on combustion.

Finally, extensive networks of pipelines transport the purified water inland, and some of it travels several hundred kilometers before it eventually reaches the capital, Riyadh. Because manufacturing fresh water demands such considerable effort, investment, and energy, every individual drop deserves to be conserved rather than wasted.

Taken as a whole, this entire sequence, from boiling or pressurizing seawater to piping the finished product across hundreds of kilometers of desert, illustrates just how much engineering effort lies hidden behind an ordinary glass of tap water in a country with so little natural fresh water of its own. Balancing the kingdom's growing demand for drinking water against the energy it consumes and the brine it produces remains an ongoing engineering challenge for the years ahead.

versions.title: From Seawater to Drinking Water
versions.text:
Standing upon the Red Sea coast, one can gaze across water that stretches uninterrupted toward the horizon, yet one could not safely drink even a single cup of it. Seawater contains such a formidable concentration of dissolved salt that its consumption would actually withdraw moisture from the body's cells through the process of osmosis, leaving the drinker considerably more dehydrated than before rather than alleviating that thirst in any way.

Approximately 97 percent of the water on this planet is located within its oceans. Of the comparatively meager remaining portion that technically qualifies as fresh water, a substantial proportion is permanently immobilized within glaciers and polar ice sheets, meaning that humanity can realistically access only an exceptionally small fraction of the planet's aggregate water supply.

Saudi Arabia possesses no permanent rivers whatsoever and receives remarkably minimal precipitation throughout the year, which means that its natural reserves of fresh water are extraordinarily constrained. Consequently, the kingdom relies substantially upon desalination, the industrial process of extracting dissolved salt from seawater, and it has become one of the foremost producers of desalinated water anywhere on the planet, operating immense facilities along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf coastlines.

The older of the two principal technologies is distillation, a method dependent fundamentally upon thermal energy input. Seawater is heated until it reaches its boiling point, and the resulting vapor ascends while the dissolved salt remains behind within the original liquid; once this vapor subsequently cools, it condenses back into usable fresh water. This procedure deliberately replicates the natural formation of rainfall, since water that evaporates naturally from the ocean likewise relinquishes its dissolved minerals during the process.

The second technology is reverse osmosis, wherein powerful pumps force seawater against a membrane, a thin synthetic sheet perforated with countless microscopic openings, while simultaneously applying tremendous hydraulic pressure. Individual water molecules are compelled through these minute openings, whereas the dissolved salt particles remain structurally incapable of passing through at all. Because reverse osmosis consumes substantially less energy than distillation, the overwhelming majority of contemporary installations now favor this particular methodology.

Both technologies inevitably generate brine, an intensely concentrated residual salt water. Facilities return this brine to the sea, but engineers must disperse it with considerable care, because a dense, undiluted accumulation can devastate the surrounding marine ecosystem, including fish populations and fragile coral reef communities that cannot withstand such extreme salinity levels.

Desalination additionally necessitates an enormous quantity of energy, much of which has historically originated from the combustion of fossil fuels. To render the process more environmentally sustainable, Saudi Arabia is experimenting with facilities powered substantially by solar energy, thereby diminishing dependence on combustion-based power generation.

Finally, extensive networks of pipelines transport the purified water inland, and a portion of it travels several hundred kilometers before eventually reaching the capital, Riyadh. Because manufacturing fresh water demands such considerable effort, capital investment, and energy expenditure, every individual drop warrants conscientious conservation rather than careless waste, a responsibility that extends to every household drawing from the municipal supply.

Considered comprehensively, this entire sequence, from the initial boiling or pressurizing of seawater to the eventual transport of the finished product across hundreds of kilometers of arid desert terrain, illustrates precisely how much sophisticated engineering effort lies concealed behind an ordinary glass of tap water in a nation possessing so little natural fresh water of its own. Reconciling the kingdom's steadily growing demand for potable water against the energy such production consumes and the brine it inevitably generates remains an ongoing and increasingly urgent engineering challenge for the decades ahead.

keyWords.example: Some cooks soak olives in brine to keep them fresh.

keyWords.definition: the power that makes machines work, such as electricity or fuel
keyWords.example: Solar panels turn sunlight into energy for the school.

questions.stem: Which sentence best tells the central idea of the article?
options: Saudi Arabia removes salt from seawater to supply drinking water, using methods that need careful planning.
Seawater is dangerous, so people should stay away from the beach.
Solar power is the cheapest kind of energy in the world.
Coral reefs in the Red Sea are the most beautiful in the world.
questions.why: The article explains why Saudi Arabia needs desalination, how the two methods work, and what problems must be managed.

wrong.B: The article says not to drink seawater, not to stay away from the beach.
wrong.C: Solar power is mentioned only as something being tested.
wrong.D: Coral is mentioned only when the article talks about brine.

questions.stem: What happens in the membrane method?
options: Seawater is boiled in large pots until all of it turns into steam.
Salt is scooped out of the water by hand.
Pumps push seawater against a thin sheet, and only water passes through.
Seawater is frozen in huge tanks so that all of the salt sinks to the bottom.
questions.why: The article says strong pumps push seawater against a membrane with tiny holes; water squeezes through, but salt cannot.

wrong.A: Boiling is the heat method, not the membrane method.
wrong.B: The article never describes removing salt by hand.
wrong.D: Freezing is not one of the methods in the article.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do most new plants choose the membrane method?
options: It makes the water taste sweet.
It uses less energy.
It does not leave any brine.
It works without pumps.
questions.why: The article says the membrane method uses less energy, so most new plants choose it.

wrong.A: The article does not say the water tastes sweet.
wrong.C: The article says both methods leave behind brine.
wrong.D: This method depends on strong pumps.

questions.stem: In the article, plants must spread out the brine carefully. What is brine?
options: Fresh water that travels inland through a long pipeline
Steam from boiling water
A tiny hole in a membrane
Very salty water left over after desalination
questions.why: The article defines brine as very salty water that both methods leave behind.

wrong.A: Pipelines carry fresh water, not brine.
wrong.B: Steam becomes fresh water when it cools.
wrong.C: The holes are part of the membrane, not brine.

questions.stem: What could happen if brine were not spread out in the sea?
options: It could harm fish and coral.
It could make the sea less salty.
It could turn into rain.
It could fill the pipelines to Riyadh.
questions.why: The article says brine must be spread out carefully so it does not harm fish and coral.

wrong.B: Brine is saltier than seawater, so it would make the water saltier, not less salty.
wrong.C: The article does not say brine becomes rain.
wrong.D: Pipelines carry fresh water inland, not brine.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the heat method to rain?
options: To show that rain is very salty
To show that the method copies how nature leaves salt behind when water rises
To explain why Saudi Arabia gets so little rain
To prove that steam is colder than seawater
questions.why: Rain forms when water rises from the sea and leaves its salt behind, which is what happens to steam in the heat method.

wrong.A: The article says rain falls as fresh drops, not salty ones.
wrong.C: The comparison is about how water loses its salt, not about weather in Saudi Arabia.
wrong.D: Steam is hot; the comparison is not about temperature.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why is Saudi Arabia testing plants that run on sunlight?
options: Because sunlight makes the water colder
Because the plants are built far away from the sea and its salt
Because desalination needs a great deal of energy
Because brine only forms at night
questions.why: The article says desalination needs a great deal of energy, so using sunshine, which Saudi Arabia has plenty of, could help.

wrong.A: Sunlight does not make the water colder.
wrong.B: The plants are on the coasts, next to the sea.
wrong.D: The article does not connect brine to night.

questions.stem: Why did the author most likely write this article?
options: To persuade readers to move to the coast
To tell a funny story about a trip to the beach
To sell a new kind of water filter
To explain how and why seawater is turned into drinking water
questions.why: The article gives facts about the need for desalination and how its two methods work.

wrong.A: The article does not ask anyone to move.
wrong.B: The beach is only an opening image; there is no funny story.
wrong.C: The article does not sell any product.

MID.prompt: Compare the heat method and the membrane method. How are they alike, and how are they different?
checklist: I described how each method takes out the salt.
I named at least one way they are alike and one way they are different.
I used key words such as membrane, pressure, or brine correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: The heat method boils seawater so steam rises and leaves the salt behind, and then the steam cools back into fresh water. The membrane method is different because pumps push seawater against a thin membrane with tiny holes, using strong pressure, so water passes through but salt cannot. Both methods are alike because they leave behind leftover brine that must be spread out carefully in the sea. One difference is that the membrane method uses less energy, which is why most new plants choose it.

keyWords.definition: a way of making a liquid pure by boiling it and cooling the vapor
keyWords.example: The scientist used distillation to separate the water from the dye.

keyWords.definition: to change from a gas into a liquid, usually by cooling
keyWords.example: Drops of water condense on a cold glass on a hot day.

keyWords.definition: the movement of water through a thin layer that blocks some other substances
keyWords.example: Plant roots take in water from the soil partly by osmosis.

keyWords.definition: all the living things in an area and the environment they share
keyWords.example: Mangrove trees are an important part of the coastal ecosystem.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without harming the environment
keyWords.example: Using cloth bags instead of plastic ones is a more sustainable habit.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Reverse osmosis will soon replace all other sources of water on Earth.
Desalination supplies Saudi Arabia with vital drinking water, but its energy use and brine must be carefully managed.
Seawater is harmful because it contains fish and coral.
Riyadh is the largest user of water in the world.
questions.why: The article explains why the kingdom relies on desalination, how it works, and the environmental and energy challenges it creates.

wrong.A: The article says most new plants prefer reverse osmosis, not that it will replace all water sources.
wrong.C: Seawater is undrinkable because of salt, not because of fish or coral.
wrong.D: The article only says water reaches Riyadh through pipelines.

questions.stem: According to the article, what happens to the steam in distillation?
options: It is pumped through a membrane.
It is mixed with brine and returned to the sea.
It cools and condenses into fresh water.
It is stored as a gas inside the pipelines.
questions.why: The article states that when the steam cools, it condenses into fresh water.

wrong.A: Membranes are used in reverse osmosis, not distillation.
wrong.B: The salt left behind becomes part of the brine; the steam becomes fresh water.
wrong.D: The pipelines carry liquid fresh water, not steam.

questions.stem: According to the article, which fact explains why most modern plants favor reverse osmosis?
options: It uses much less energy than distillation.
It produces no brine.
It requires no pumps.
It works only with water from the Arabian Gulf.
questions.why: The article states that reverse osmosis consumes considerably less energy than distillation.

wrong.B: The article says both methods generate brine.
wrong.C: Reverse osmosis depends on powerful pumps.
wrong.D: The article says plants operate on both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf.

questions.stem: The article says Saudi Arabia wants to make desalination more sustainable. What does sustainable mean here?
options: Faster to build
Able to continue without harming the environment
Cheaper to sell to other countries around the world
Saltier and more concentrated
questions.why: The article links the word to replacing fossil fuels with solar energy, which suggests a process that can last without damaging the environment.

wrong.A: The article does not discuss how quickly plants are built.
wrong.C: Selling water abroad is not mentioned.
wrong.D: That describes brine, not a sustainable process.

questions.stem: What is the effect of releasing a dense layer of undiluted brine into the sea?
options: It can damage the marine ecosystem, including coral reefs.
It makes the seawater much easier for the next plant to desalinate.
It turns the brine back into fresh water.
It produces solar energy for the plant.
questions.why: The article warns that a dense layer of brine can damage the marine ecosystem, including fish and coral reefs.

wrong.B: Saltier water would not make desalination easier, and the article does not say this.
wrong.C: Brine does not become fresh water in the sea.
wrong.D: Solar energy comes from sunlight, not brine.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that much fresh water is locked in glaciers and ice sheets?
options: To explain why the oceans are so salty
To argue that Saudi Arabia should start buying and shipping in ice from cold lands
To show that usable fresh water is even scarcer than it first seems
To describe how distillation works
questions.why: If much of the small share of fresh water is frozen, people can reach only a tiny fraction, which strengthens the case for desalination.

wrong.A: Frozen fresh water does not explain ocean salt.
wrong.B: The article never suggests importing ice.
wrong.D: Distillation is explained later and does not involve glaciers.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer about Saudi Arabia's choice to use solar energy?
options: It will make the brine less salty.
It means pipelines will no longer be needed.
It is meant to stop fish from entering the plants.
It could reduce the burning of fossil fuels needed for desalination.
questions.why: The article says much of the energy traditionally came from fossil fuels, so solar energy could reduce that need.

wrong.A: Energy source does not change how salty the brine is.
wrong.B: Water would still need to be carried inland through pipelines.
wrong.C: The article does not connect solar energy to fish.

questions.stem: How does the article organize its information about the two desalination technologies?
options: It tells the life story of an engineer.
It describes each method in turn and then compares their energy use.
It lists water prices in different cities.
It presents arguments for and against living near the sea.
questions.why: The article explains distillation, then reverse osmosis, and states that reverse osmosis uses less energy than distillation.

wrong.C: The article does not mention prices.
wrong.D: The article does not debate where people should live.

HIGH.prompt: Desalination solves one problem but creates others. Using evidence from the article, explain the benefits and the challenges of desalination, and suggest which challenge matters most.
checklist: I explained at least one benefit and two challenges using facts from the article.
I chose the challenge I think matters most and gave a reason.
I used precise words such as distillation, ecosystem, or sustainable correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Desalination gives Saudi Arabia a reliable water supply even though the country has no rivers and receives almost no rainfall. However, it also creates serious challenges: both distillation and the membrane method demand an enormous amount of energy, and the leftover brine can threaten the marine ecosystem if it is not dispersed carefully. In my view, the energy demand matters most, because an energy-hungry process is not truly sustainable unless it is powered by something renewable, which is why I think the new solar-powered plants are such an important step.
